soil-env-236.title: Pesticide leaching: the slow trip to groundwater
soil-env-236.text: A pesticide that dissolves can travel far beyond the field it was meant for. Pesticide leaching is that movement of dissolved pesticides down through the soil, a major source of groundwater pollution. Three things decide it: the soil, the pesticide, and the rainfall and irrigation. It is worst for water-soluble pesticides that cling weakly to soil, on sandy soils, and when heavy watering follows soon after spraying. Treated fields are not the only source. Mixing areas, machinery-washing sites and disposal areas leak too.

soil-env-258.title: Five ways to deal with metal-polluted soil
soil-env-258.text: Metals never break down, so cleanup must move them, trap them or change them. The remediation of metal-contaminated soil has five broad routes. Isolation quarantines the soil with caps, membranes or buried barriers. Immobilization alters the soil itself so metals cannot travel. Toxicity reduction oxidizes or reduces metal ions, chemically or biologically, into less toxic or less mobile forms. Physical separation sorts them out of the soil, and extraction pulls them out with chemicals, high-temperature volatilization or electrolysis, on or off site. The contaminant and the site decide which fits.

soil-env-256.title: Cadmium poisoning: a metal that stays for decades
soil-env-256.text: Cadmium settles into bone and stays, with a biological half-life of about 30 years. Cadmium poisoning comes from a naturally occurring toxic metal met in industry, in plant soils and in tobacco smoke. Farming can add to it: some phosphate fertilizers carry up to 100 mg/kg cadmium, which builds up in soil. Chronic exposure softens and weakens bones and permanently damages the kidneys, which can shrink by up to 30 percent. Daily intake is about 8 to 30 μg in Europe and the US. In parts of Japan, where people ate rice irrigated with contaminated water, it reached 59 to 113 μg.

soil-env-247.title: Bioslurping: sipping oil off the water table
soil-env-247.text: Bioslurping works like a straw dipped into floating fuel. It combines {{ref:soil-env-024}} with vacuum pumping of free product, the LNAPL floating on groundwater. A slurp tube reaching into the fuel layer draws up liquid and soil gas together. It lifts oil off the water table and the capillary fringe, the damp band just above it. Meanwhile air pulled into the unsaturated zone feeds microbes that break down the remaining hydrocarbons aerobically.

soil-env-248.title: Dual-phase extraction: one well for water and vapor
soil-env-248.text: The dirtiest layer at a spill is often the thin damp band just above the water table, the capillary fringe. Dual-phase vacuum extraction, also called multi-phase extraction, reaches it with a high vacuum. A single well removes both contaminated groundwater and soil vapor. Pumping lowers the water table and exposes the fringe. {{ref:soil-env-045}} then draws its contaminants out. Treating that layer can shorten the cleanup of a site.

soil-env-223.title: Pneumatic fracturing: cracking the ground to clean it
soil-env-223.text: Tight ground keeps its pollution. Pneumatic fracturing breaks it open by injecting gas at a pressure above that of the gases already present. The fractures spread like a spider web. Pumps can then draw contaminated water out through the cracks. The same cracks carry injected substrates that speed the cleanup of soil and groundwater.

soil-env-224.title: Total petroleum hydrocarbons: one number for crude oil
soil-env-224.text: Crude oil holds several hundred hydrocarbon compounds, far too many to measure one by one at a spill. Total petroleum hydrocarbon, or TPH, solves this by measuring them all as a single total. It adds the volatile, gasoline-range compounds, with six to ten carbon atoms (C6–C10), to the extractable ones. Diesel-range organics span C10–C28. The mix includes hexane, benzene, toluene, xylenes, naphthalene and fluorene.

soil-env-229.title: Electrical resistance heating: boiling pollutants out
soil-env-229.text: Electrical resistance heating turns the ground into a kettle. Alternating current runs between buried electrodes, and the soil's resistance heats it until water boils at depth. The steam strips out volatile contaminants, which a vapor recovery system captures and treats at the surface. It works best on volatile compounds such as perchloroethylene and trichloroethylene; diesel needs more energy. Current flows through the thin water film on grains, so it works in any soil and in sedimentary bedrock. Electrodes typically sit 15 to 20 feet apart, and runs last under a year.

soil-env-232.title: Microbial biodegradation: putting microbes to work on pollution
soil-env-232.text: For years, scientists doubted that hydrocarbons and halogenated compounds could break down without oxygen. Then bacteria that do exactly that were isolated. Microbial biodegradation harnesses microbes' natural ability to degrade, transform or accumulate pollutants, from oil, PCBs and PAHs to pharmaceuticals, radionuclides and metals. Bioavailability, the share of a pollutant microbes can physically reach, is key. In one study, most soil clays, kaolinite excepted, slowed bacterial breakdown of 2-picoline by adsorbing it. At sea, hydrocarbon-degrading bacteria remove a considerable share of the petroleum that enters.

soil-env-260.title: Ecotoxicity tests: how hazard gets a number
soil-env-260.text: How toxic is a chemical to an earthworm? Ecotoxicity testing answers with standardized acute and chronic tests on soil and aquatic organisms, including {{ref:soil-bio-040}}. LC50 is the concentration that kills 50% of test organisms within the test, which can last up to 96 hours. EC50 is the concentration causing an adverse effect in 50% of them. NOEC is the highest dose with no statistically significant effect. Acute toxicity below 1 part per million puts a substance in Class I, 1–10 ppm in Class II and 10–100 ppm in Class III.

soil-env-239.title: Breakdown products that outlive the pesticide
soil-env-239.text: A pesticide's breakdown is not always the end of the story. Its transformation products can keep, or even exceed, the parent's harmful activity. Smaller and more polar than the parent, they reach groundwater and surface water more readily. Europe sorts these metabolites as nonrelevant, groundwater-relevant or ecotoxicologically relevant. A metabolite is groundwater-relevant when it is likely above 0.1 μg/liter and as toxic as its parent. Allowing up to 10 μg/liter of nonrelevant metabolites in groundwater is disputed. Some see no proven health risk; others see a breach of the precautionary principle.

soil-env-264.title: How soil microbes eat spilled oil
soil-env-264.text: Up to twenty percent of soil microbes can live on petroleum. Hydrocarbon biodegradation in soil is their breakdown of these compounds for energy and carbon, mostly with oxygen, ending in carbon dioxide and water. Structure decides speed. Long straight chains degrade most readily; short, branched and quaternary ones less so. Ring compounds with two or three rings break down at useful rates. Those with four or more resist, yielding only to cometabolism, breakdown alongside another food. Porous, carbon-rich biochar traps {{ref:soil-env-199}} and gives microbes good conditions to degrade them.

soil-env-263.title: The Raymond process: feeding microbes in a loop
soil-env-263.text: Richard Raymond devised a way to speed up {{ref:soil-env-262}} by feeding the microbes underground. Groundwater is pumped up downstream of the contamination, infused with nutrients and oxygen, and re-injected upstream. The loop repeats. The oxygen serves as the {{ref:soil-chem-176}} the microbes need. It can arrive through injection wells or galleries, or as ozone, half of which turns to oxygen within twenty minutes.

soil-env-228.title: Breaking down PCBs takes two teams of microbes
soil-env-228.text: PCBs, once used as dielectric fluids and coolants, are stable, poorly soluble {{ref:soil-env-198}}. Natural degradation takes 3 to 37 years, depending on how chlorinated they are. Bioremediation of PCBs uses microbes in sequence. Anaerobic bacteria first strip off chlorine, using PCBs as electron acceptors. Aerobic microbes then break the products down. The job is hard: PCBs bind tightly to soil, especially soil rich in organic carbon and clay. They are toxic to bacteria above 1000 mg/kg, and breakdown slows sharply below 50 mg/kg.

soil-env-268.title: Geochemical background: what counts as normal
soil-env-268.text: To call soil contaminated, you first need to know what is natural there. Geochemical background is the natural level of elements and other substances in soil, water and air, set by processes such as {{ref:soil-found-052}}. Typical soils hold no more than about 100 mg/kg of arsenic, lead and nickel, 2 mg/kg of cadmium, 150 mg/kg of copper and 300 mg/kg of zinc. Chromium stays under 500 mg/kg and selenium under 1 mg/kg. Remediation results are compared with these local levels as well as zoning standards, and {{ref:soil-env-287}} makes setting them a priority.

soil-env-261.title: Emerging contaminants: pollutants the rules have not caught
soil-env-261.text: Monitoring keeps finding pollutants that no law yet covers. Contaminants of emerging concern may harm ecosystems or health and are usually unregulated. They include pharmaceuticals, personal care products, industrial byproducts and agricultural chemicals, which often escape detection and treatment and persist. Runoff after rain or irrigation carries pesticides and pharmaceuticals from soil into rivers, lakes and groundwater. Treatment must not just shift them into sludge, since sludge spread on land returns them. Explosives such as TNT are major contaminants of groundwater and soils.

soil-env-265.title: Living cleanup crews for radioactive soil
soil-env-265.text: Digging up radioactive soil and hauling it far away could cost the US more than a trillion dollars. Bioremediation of radioactive waste offers another route. Bacteria, plants and fungi catalyze reactions that change radionuclides' solubility, availability and mobility, speeding their stabilization. The commonest natural radionuclides in soils are radium-226, radon-222, thorium-232, uranium-238 and potassium-40. Some fungi can even use ionizing radiation as energy. Oyster mushrooms can bioremediate plutonium-239 and americium-241.

soil-env-266.title: Bioreduction: bacteria that pin uranium in place
soil-env-266.text: Bacteria can turn dissolved uranium into a solid. In bioreduction, their enzymes reduce radionuclides to lower oxidation states, changing their solubility, mobility and radiotoxicity. Anaerobes use the radioisotope as the final electron acceptor, reducing soluble uranium(VI) to insoluble uranium(IV). Sulfate-reducing and metal-reducing bacteria also act indirectly, through the metabolites they excrete. Microbes can work the other way too. Siderophores and other bacterial chelators raise radionuclide solubility and availability.

soil-env-267.title: Plants that pull radioactivity from soil
soil-env-267.text: In the Chernobyl zone, mustard greens removed up to 22% of average caesium activity in one growing season. Phytoextraction of radionuclides uses plants that carry them from the roots into the shoots. It works for caesium-137, strontium-90, technetium-99, plutonium-240 and americium-241, among others. It leaves soil structure and fertility largely intact and suits large areas of low-level contamination. The catch is that it needs plants that grow big, fast.

soil-env-226.title: Sustainable remediation: a cleanup should not do more harm
soil-env-226.text: A cleanup can sometimes hurt more than the pollution. Pump-and-treat and dig-and-haul have at times left lasting side effects worse than the contamination itself. Sustainable remediation weighs a remedy's environmental, economic and social effects and shrinks the footprint of the cleanup. Footprint analysis covers energy, air and atmosphere, materials and waste, land and ecosystem, and water. The stakes are large: the US alone has more than 450,000 brownfield sites needing major reinvestment. Some newer in situ methods have cut life-cycle greenhouse gas emissions by 50 to 80 percent.

soil-env-225.title: Vapor intrusion: pollution that seeps indoors
soil-env-225.text: Contaminated groundwater can poison the air inside a house. Vapor intrusion is the migration of volatile chemicals, usually VOCs, from soil or groundwater into buildings above or nearby. The vapors diffuse up through the porous {{ref:soil-water-230}} and enter through foundation cracks, drawn in by the building's stack effect. Pipes, storm drains and elevator shafts offer easy paths. Indoors they can cause headaches, raise the risk of some cancers and even threaten explosion. Fixes include a fan that depressurizes the space under the slab, or over-pressurizing the building.
